slides.title: The Compute Instance Explained
slides.body:
The Compute Instance
Subheading: Unit Of Compute
A hypervisor is software that lets one physical host run many separate virtual machines. An instance is one such virtual machine — the smallest billable unit of compute in the cloud.
Bundles virtual CPU (vCPU), memory, network and storage together
Each instance gets a unique instance ID at launch
Moves through lifecycle states: pending, running, stopped, terminated
One instance is one isolated compute boundary per workload
Analogy: Renting a hotel room for exactly the nights needed, paying only while checked in — just as an instance is billed only while it is provisioned and running.
Visual Guidance: Diagram: a physical host box with a hypervisor layer, one highlighted VM box labelled Instance showing vCPU, memory, network and storage icons.
slides.notes: Explain that an instance bundles compute, memory and storage into one billable unit. Point out the lifecycle states as a common exam question. Mention EC2 as the AWS name for this unit.

slides.title: How Provisioning Happens
slides.body:
Provisioning Mechanism
Subheading: Request To Running
Provisioning is the automated path from a request to a running instance — a console click or a programmatic call triggers allocation, not weeks of physical setup.
Request names the image, instance type and network settings
Scheduler picks a physical host with free capacity
Hypervisor boots the virtual machine from the chosen image
Instance becomes reachable once status checks pass
AWS exposes this as the EC2 console
Or as the launch Application Programming Interface (API) call
Visual Guidance: Left-to-right flow diagram: Request, Scheduler, Hypervisor Boot, Status Check, Running, with arrows between each stage.
slides.notes: Walk through the four steps from request to a reachable instance. Name the EC2 console and the RunInstances API as where this happens in AWS. Ask what happens between clicking launch and the instance becoming reachable.

slides.title: Provisioning In Practice
slides.body:
Provisioning In AWS
Subheading: Where Billing Begins
This on-demand provisioning is what makes elasticity possible: capacity is requested and released in minutes, turning compute into a metered utility rather than a fixed purchase.
Launched via the EC2 console or infrastructure automation tools
Billing starts the moment the instance enters Running state
Terminating an instance returns its capacity to the shared pool
Stopped instances stop compute charges but keep storage billed
No separate provisioning fee is charged at all
Visual Guidance: Small mockup of an EC2 console Launch Instance button beside a lifecycle bar running from Pending to Running to Terminated.
slides.notes: Stress that billing starts only at Running, not Pending. Point to the lifecycle bar on the diagram. Ask what happens to cost if an instance is left Stopped rather than Terminated.

slides.title: Choosing An Instance For A Workload
slides.body:
Sizing One Workload
Subheading: Picking An Instance
A low-traffic web app and a CPU-heavy batch job need different instances, since provisioning lets each request exactly the capacity its load demands.
Visual Guidance: Side-by-side cards: t3.micro labelled Web App, c5.large labelled Batch Job, each showing vCPU and memory values.
slides.notes: Walk through why the batch job needs sustained compute while the web app only needs light, bursty capacity. Point to the table's vCPU and memory columns. Ask which instance type fits a steady, heavy workload.

slides.title: EC2 Instance Family Landscape
slides.body:
Instance Families Overview
Subheading: Five Resource-Based Types
EC2 instance types are grouped into families, each built around the one resource — compute, memory, storage, or specialised hardware — that its workloads lean on most.
General purpose: balanced vCPU-to-memory ratio for mixed workloads
Compute optimized: high vCPU-to-memory ratio for CPU-bound tasks
Memory optimized: large RAM-to-vCPU ratio for in-memory workloads
Storage optimized: fast local disks for I/O-heavy tasks
GPU & accelerator: dedicated chips for AI/ML training and inference
Visual Guidance: Five labelled boxes in a row — General Purpose, Compute, Memory, Storage, GPU/Accelerator — each with a small icon (scale, chip, RAM stick, disk, GPU).
slides.notes: Present this as the map of families before going into any one of them in detail. Mention that AWS, Azure and GCP all group instance types this same way, just with different naming letters.

slides.title: General Purpose Instances Explained
slides.body:
General Purpose Family
Subheading: Balanced Resource Mix
General purpose instances, AWS's M-family, keep virtual CPU (vCPU) count and memory in a near-equal ratio, so no single resource is starved for typical mixed workloads.
Typical use: web servers, small-to-medium databases, dev environments
Moderately priced: a sensible default when the main bottleneck is not yet known
Analogy: A general-purpose instance is like a family sedan car — not the fastest, not the biggest boot, but balanced for most everyday trips — just as it balances CPU and memory instead of maximising either.
Visual Guidance: A balance scale with 'vCPU' on one pan and 'Memory' on the other, level, labelled M-family.
slides.notes: Explain that balanced does not mean weak; it means no bottleneck is designed in advance. Ask: why would a web server rarely need the heaviest memory or CPU ratio?

slides.title: Compute Optimized Instances
slides.body:
Compute Optimized Family
Subheading: High CPU Ratio
Compute optimized instances shift the balance toward more vCPU per gigabyte of memory, suiting workloads bottlenecked purely by processing speed rather than data volume.
Typical use: batch processing, gaming servers, scientific simulation
Resource ratio: high vCPU count relative to memory size
AWS example: the C-family instance types
Cost: priced for CPU throughput, not memory capacity
Visual Guidance: Same balance-scale image as the general purpose slide, now tilted heavily toward the vCPU side, labelled C-family.
slides.notes: Contrast directly with the general purpose ratio shown earlier on the same scale image. Point out video encoding and simulation as the canonical interview example of a CPU-bound job.

slides.title: Memory And Storage Optimized Families
slides.body:
Memory & Storage Families
Subheading: RAM And Disk Focus
Memory optimized instances favour RAM-heavy workloads, while storage optimized instances favour fast local-disk access — two separate bottlenecks that general purpose and compute families do not target.
Visual Guidance: Two-column spec table rendered directly from the comparison; no extra diagram needed.
slides.notes: Clarify that storage optimized local disks are ephemeral, unlike the persistent EBS block volumes used for durable data. Point to this table when contrasting memory-heavy and disk-heavy workloads. Exam angle: ask which family suits a Cassandra-style database needing heavy disk I/O.

slides.title: GPU And Accelerator Families
slides.body:
GPU Accelerator Family
Subheading: Built For AI/ML
GPU and accelerator instances attach a graphics processing unit (GPU) or a purpose-built AI chip beside the CPU, giving the massively parallel compute that AI/ML workloads need.
Use case: deep learning training, large-scale inference, rendering
AWS example: P-family for training, G-family for inference/graphics
Cost: priced well above CPU-only families per running hour
Analogy: A GPU is like an exam hall with hundreds of invigilators checking answer sheets at once, instead of one teacher checking them one by one — just as thousands of GPU cores process data in parallel instead of a CPU working sequentially.
Visual Guidance: A CPU chip icon next to a larger GPU chip icon made of many small grid cells, labelled P-family and G-family.
slides.notes: Stress that a GPU instance is still an EC2 instance, just with specialised hardware attached. The memory constraint this hardware introduces is covered separately under sizing.

slides.title: Choosing The Right Instance Family
slides.body:
Choosing A Family
Subheading: Matching Workload To Type
Selecting a family starts with naming the workload's actual bottleneck — balanced, CPU, memory, disk, or parallel compute — then matching it to the family built for that exact bottleneck.
Visual Guidance: The five-family row from the first slide, now with an arrow from each workload signal in the table pointing to its matching box.
slides.notes: Close by noting that picking the family is only step one; right-sizing within that family is the next decision. A specialised, more expensive family left idle wastes money faster than an under-sized general purpose one.

slides.title: Dimensions Of Instance Sizing
slides.body:
Sizing Dimensions
Subheading: Four Key Axes
Choosing an instance size means balancing four characteristics together, not picking one number.
vCPU: virtual CPU cores allocated to the instance
Memory: RAM available for applications and caches
Network: bandwidth for data transfer, measured in Gbps
Storage: IOPS and throughput to attached EBS volumes
Visual Guidance: Four-quadrant diagram: vCPU, Memory, Network, Storage icons arranged around a central instance box.
slides.notes: Introduce the four axes learners will size against before taking each one in turn. Interview angle: naming all four dimensions when asked how to size an instance.

slides.title: vCPU and Memory Explained
slides.body:
vCPU & Memory
Subheading: Compute And RAM
A virtual CPU (vCPU) is a thread of a physical processor core assigned to one instance; memory is the RAM it can address directly.
vCPU count sets how many parallel threads the instance runs
Memory size limits data held in RAM before swapping or failure
m6i.xlarge offers 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB memory
Burstable instances (T-family) earn CPU credits to run above a baseline CPU level
Analogy: A vCPU is like one worker at a counter and memory is the counter space available — just as more workers need more counter space, more vCPUs need more memory to avoid contention.
Visual Guidance: Bar chart comparing vCPU count and memory size for two instance sizes side by side.
slides.notes: Explain vCPU as a thread, not a full physical core, and memory as the shared workspace it works in. Point to the m6i.xlarge figures as a concrete reference. Exam hook: vCPU versus physical core distinction.

slides.title: Network and Storage Specs
slides.body:
Network & Storage
Subheading: Bandwidth And IOPS
Network and storage characteristics decide how fast data moves to the instance and its attached disks, independent of vCPU or memory.
Network bandwidth: measured in Gbps, scales with instance size
Baseline bandwidth can burst higher for short periods
EBS-optimized throughput: dedicated MB/s bandwidth to attached volumes
IOPS: input/output operations per second a volume sustains
Visual Guidance: Instance box with two labelled arrows: network bandwidth in Gbps to the internet, EBS throughput in MB/s to a disk icon.
slides.notes: Clarify that EBS-optimized bandwidth is separate from general network bandwidth, so a storage-heavy job can bottleneck with spare vCPU still free. Exam hook: difference between network Gbps and EBS throughput MB/s.

slides.title: Right-Sizing An Instance
slides.body:
Right-Sizing
Subheading: Matching Size To Load
Right-sizing means picking the smallest instance that meets sustained CPU, memory, network and storage needs, checked against real usage data.
AWS Compute Optimizer analyses CloudWatch metrics for sizing recommendations
Over-provisioning pays for idle capacity every billing hour
Under-provisioning causes throttling, swapping or dropped network packets
Resize by stopping, changing instance type, then restarting
Visual Guidance: Gauge chart with three zones: under-provisioned, right-sized, over-provisioned.
slides.notes: Stress that right-sizing is a recurring check as workload patterns shift, not a one-time launch decision. Reserved pricing only pays off once utilization stays consistently high. Exam hook: name the AWS tool used for sizing recommendations.

slides.title: VRAM: The AI Sizing Constraint
slides.body:
VRAM Constraint
Subheading: GPU Memory Limit
Video RAM (VRAM) is the dedicated memory on a GPU that holds model weights and data during AI training or inference, separate from the instance's system RAM.
VRAM capacity caps the model size a GPU can load
Exceeding VRAM causes an out-of-memory failure, not slowdown
g5.xlarge: one NVIDIA A10G GPU with 24 GB VRAM
g4dn.xlarge: one NVIDIA T4 GPU with 16 GB VRAM
Analogy: A workbench of fixed size cannot hold a job bigger than itself, however strong the worker — just as a model exceeding VRAM cannot load, regardless of GPU speed.
Visual Guidance: Two GPU cards labelled with VRAM capacity, and a model-size bar that fits one card and overflows the other.
slides.notes: Emphasise VRAM as a hard ceiling, not a performance dial like vCPU or memory. Point to the two GPU figures as sizing references. Exam hook: why VRAM overflow fails outright instead of degrading gracefully.

slides.title: Sizing A Workload: Worked Case
slides.body:
Worked Sizing Case
Subheading: Two Workload Types
Two workloads illustrate the same sizing method: a web application bound by vCPU and memory, and an inference job bound by VRAM.
Visual Guidance: Two cards side by side: left card shows m6i.xlarge specs for the web app, right card shows g5.xlarge specs for the inference job.
slides.notes: Walk through both rows: the web app fits comfortably on m6i.xlarge, while the inference job needs the larger VRAM of the A10G GPU, not just more vCPUs. Exam hook: explain why g4dn.xlarge fails the 18 GB model despite having free vCPU capacity.
tables: Matches vCPU and memory, avoids idle capacity cost

slides.title: Sizing Recap
slides.body:
Sizing Recap
Subheading: Four Axes Chosen
Matching vCPU, memory, network and storage to real load — with VRAM as a separate hard ceiling for AI workloads — keeps compute cost proportional to need.
vCPU and memory sized to sustained CPU/RAM demand
Network and storage sized to data movement rate
VRAM sized separately, as a strict GPU memory limit
Visual Guidance: Four icons — vCPU, Memory, Network/Storage, VRAM — each with a checkmark, leading toward an image/provisioning icon.
slides.notes: Summarise the four sizing axes together before provisioning with a machine image is taught. Exam hook: list all sizing axes, including VRAM, from memory as a quick self-test.

slides.title: Images Provisioning Landscape
slides.body:
Provisioning Building Blocks
Subheading: Three Launch Inputs
Launching a compute instance needs more than picking a size: it needs a starting operating system, a way to run setup automatically, and a way to log in securely.
Machine image: OS and software template the instance boots from
User data: script that bootstraps the instance on first boot
Key pair: public/private credential for secure access
All three are chosen together when the instance is launched
Visual Guidance: Three labelled boxes — Machine Image, User Data, Key Pair — feeding into one 'Instance Launch' box.
slides.notes: Frame this as the three decisions made at launch time, beyond just size. Ask: which of these three decides what software is already installed? Point out each will get its own slide.

slides.title: Machine Images Explained
slides.body:
What Machine Images Are
Subheading: AMI Template
A machine image is a saved template of an operating system plus installed software and configuration. On AWS it is called an AMI (Amazon Machine Image), and launching from it gives every instance an identical starting state.
Provider images: pre-built, maintained OS templates (Amazon Linux, Ubuntu)
Custom images: captured from a configured running instance
Marketplace images: vendor-packaged software bundled with an OS
Images are tied to one region and must be copied to launch elsewhere
Analogy: A machine image is like a recipe card with every ingredient pre-measured — just as every instance launched from it starts in the exact same state, with nothing improvised.
Visual Guidance: One AMI box branching into multiple identical instance boxes, each labelled 'same OS, same software'.
slides.notes: Emphasise 'identical starting state' as the exam-testable idea, not just 'it has an OS'. Mention that a custom AMI is how a configured server becomes repeatable. Interview angle: why would a team build its own AMI instead of using the provider's base image?

slides.title: User Data And Bootstrapping
slides.body:
User Data Script
Subheading: First-Boot Automation
User data is a script supplied at launch time that the instance runs automatically once it boots, replacing manual setup after the instance appears.
Passed as plain text or shell commands at launch time
Executed by the instance's boot-time init process once
Runs only on first boot, not on every subsequent restart
Typical use: install packages, pull application code, start a service
Visual Guidance: Timeline: Launch → First Boot → User Data Script Runs → Application Ready; grey out a second 'Reboot' box with 'script skipped'.
slides.notes: Stress 'once, at first boot' — a common exam trap is assuming it reruns on every restart. Give the example of a script that installs a web server before anyone connects. Ask: how does a team re-run setup if the instance reboots?

slides.title: Key Pairs For Access
slides.body:
Key Pair Access
Subheading: Public Private Keys
Cloud instances replace password login with a key pair, two mathematically linked keys that let an owner prove identity without ever sending a password over the network.
Public key: installed into the instance's authorized list at launch
Private key: downloaded once by the owner, never stored by the provider again
Password-based login is disabled by default on cloud OS images
A lost private key means lost access unless a new key is attached
Analogy: A key pair works like a locker whose lock the renter alone can open — the facility keeps only the lock pattern, never a copy of the key — just as the instance holds only the public key, never the private one.
Visual Guidance: Two padlock icons: Public Key on the instance, Private Key on the user's laptop, with a matching arrow between them.
slides.notes: Clarify this is asymmetric cryptography applied to login, not encryption of data. Point out the private key download is one-time only. Interview hook: why can't the provider recover a lost private key?

slides.title: Provisioning Sequence Combined
slides.body:
Launch Sequence
Subheading: Image Data Key
Launching an instance chains the three building blocks into one sequence: the image decides what boots, the key pair decides who can log in, and user data decides what runs next.
Visual Guidance: Flow arrow left to right across the four table rows, ending in a green 'Instance Ready' box.
slides.notes: Walk the table row by row as the actual launch order. Note the AWS console surfaces all three on the same launch screen. Mention this sequence is identical whether the instance is launched manually or by an auto scaling group.
tables: Who can log in, and how
What gets configured on first boot

slides.title: Provisioning Recap Bridge
slides.body:
Provisioning Recap
Subheading: Toward Scaling
A correctly provisioned instance pairs a known image with a bootstrap script and a secure key, giving every instance a predictable, repeatable starting point.
Image fixes the software baseline before any script runs
User data removes manual post-launch configuration
Key pair replaces passwords with asymmetric credentials
Repeatable launch configuration is what automated scaling will reuse
Visual Guidance: Single consolidated box labelled 'Launch Configuration' with the three inputs feeding in, and an arrow pointing off-slide toward 'Auto Scaling'.
slides.notes: Close by noting a repeatable launch configuration is exactly what scaling will need to launch instances without manual steps. No new facts here — just tie the three pieces together.

slides.title: Auto Scaling Groups And Launch Templates
slides.body:
Scaling The Fleet
Subheading: ASG And Templates
An auto scaling group (ASG) keeps a fleet of instances at the right size automatically, using a launch template as the blueprint for every new instance it starts.
Scaling policies: rules deciding when to add or remove instances
Health checks: detect and replace unhealthy instances automatically
Capacity limits: minimum, maximum and desired instance counts
Spans multiple availability zones for resilience
Visual Guidance: Diagram: ASG box pulling from a Launch Template, spawning instances between Min and Max markers, with a scaling policy arrow and a health-check loop.
slides.notes: Frame the ASG as the fleet manager and the launch template as its recipe card. Point out that every part named here gets its own detail on the next slides. Exam hook: ASG without a launch template cannot launch anything.

slides.title: Launch Templates And Versioning
slides.body:
Launch Templates
Subheading: Versioned Blueprint
Launching instances by hand means repeating the same setup each time. A launch template stores that configuration — Amazon Machine Image (AMI), instance type, key pair and security group — as a reusable, versioned blueprint the auto scaling group reads whenever it starts a new instance.
Each edit creates a new numbered version
Auto scaling group launches from the version it is set to use: default, latest or a fixed number
Rolling back means pointing the group at a prior version
Replaces the older, non-versioned launch configuration format
Analogy: A launch template is like a builder's standard house plan: every house built from it gets the same layout and door locks — just as every instance launched gets the same AMI, instance type and security group from the template.
Visual Guidance: Show a template box with version tags v1, v2, v3 and an arrow from the default version into a newly launched instance.
slides.notes: Stress that editing a template never changes running instances — it only affects future launches. Ask: how would a bad new version be rolled back without touching live traffic? Mention this is what the ASG actually reads at launch time.

slides.title: Capacity Limits And Scaling Policies
slides.body:
Scaling Policies
Subheading: How ASG Reacts
Capacity sits between a minimum and maximum; a scaling policy decides how many instances run at any moment inside that range, and a cooldown stops it reacting too fast.
Desired capacity: the current target instance count maintained
Health check grace period: wait before marking an instance unhealthy
Cooldown period: pause between scaling actions to let changes settle
Cost: new capacity is billed only while it actually runs
Visual Guidance: Horizontal bar from Min to Max capacity with a Desired marker sliding inside it, three small icons above the table row labelling each policy type.
slides.notes: Walk through why target tracking suits steady load while scheduled scaling suits predictable daily patterns. Point at the cooldown bullet when explaining why a group does not scale on every single data point. Exam hook: step scaling needs defined step adjustments, target tracking does not.
tables: Keeps a metric near a set value
Scale up every weekday at 9 AM

slides.title: What Gets Built Today
slides.body:
Practical Overview
Subheading: EC2 Plus Beanstalk
This practical launches a general-purpose EC2 instance and then deploys a small Flask application on Elastic Beanstalk, so the instance-as-unit-of-compute idea and the managed-platform provisioning model are both seen running live.
1. Sign in to the AWS console and select the Mumbai region
2. Launch an EC2 instance with a chosen AMI and size
3. Connect to the instance and run basic verification commands
4. Package a small Flask application as a ZIP archive
5. Create an Elastic Beanstalk application and environment from the ZIP
6. Deploy and verify Version 1, then update to Version 2
7. Clean up every resource created to avoid charges

slides.title: Launching the EC2 Instance
slides.body:
EC2 Instance Launch
Subheading: Image and Sizing Choices
The instance launches from a machine image on a general-purpose size, with a security group allowing only the learner's own IP for remote access.
s9-ec2-vm-demo in Running state with 3/3 status checks passed
AMI Amazon Linux 2023 on a t3.micro instance
Key pair s9-ec2-key for access
Security group s9-ec2-sg allowing SSH (port 22) from My IP only

slides.title: Connecting and Verifying the VM
slides.body:
Instance Connect
Subheading: Confirming Access
A browser-based terminal opens on the instance through EC2 Instance Connect, and basic Linux commands confirm access.
whoami, hostname, uname -a and os-release output on the instance

slides.title: Packaging the Application
slides.body:
Application Packaging
Subheading: Files Before Upload
The Flask application file and dependency list are archived in a ZIP with both files at the root, not inside a folder.
application.py and requirements.txt in the s9-paas-demo folder

slides.title: Deploying Version 1
slides.body:
Beanstalk Environment
Subheading: First Deployment Live
The ZIP is uploaded to a new Elastic Beanstalk environment on the Python platform, which provisions and manages the servers for us, unlike the EC2 VM we managed ourselves.
S9-paas-demo-env with Health Ok

slides.title: Updating to Version 2
slides.body:
Version Update
Subheading: Redeploy and Confirm
The code is updated, re-zipped as Version 2 and deployed to the same environment, with no new server created.
Version 2 page served at the same environment URL
Verify that the Version 2 page loads at the same URL and the running version is the latest upload
Clean up to avoid charges: terminate the EC2 instance and the Elastic Beanstalk environment
Then delete security group s9-ec2-sg and check for leftover EBS volumes and public IPs

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
1. Compute in the Cloud: The instance as the unit of compute; the provisioning model
2. Instance Families: General purpose, compute, memory & storage optimized; GPU & accelerator families for AI/ML
3. Sizing & Selection: vCPU, memory, network & storage characteristics; right-sizing; VRAM as the AI constraint
4. Images & Provisioning: Machine images; user data & bootstrapping; key pairs & instance access
5. Scaling: Auto scaling groups & launch templates
